The Block-based Ray Cache is a memory optimization technique for volume rendering that reduces reconstruction overhead by retaining reconstructed voxel blocks in memory for reuse by adjacent rays.
It solves the problem of redundant computation in high-resolution volume rendering where data exceeds physical memory, allowing rendering times to drop from days to minutes.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly maintaining a sorted list of blocks along the ray depth to facilitate immediate lookup, rather than relying solely on generic LRU eviction without spatial locality awareness.
Choose it when adjacent rays share heavy reconstruction workloads.
This method couples LRU brick cache eviction with hierarchical residency octree updates.
When the cache lacks a free slot, it evicts the least recently accessed brick and resets bitmask entries in affected leaf and non-leaf nodes to reflect the loss of resident data.
It differs from standard LRU caches by synchronizing cache state with octree metadata after each eviction.
Choose it when maintaining strict consistency between cache residency and hierarchical traversal structures is required.
The Brick Cache is a single-channel 3D texture cache that stores bricks from a multi-resolution multi-volume hierarchy.
It is agnostic to the number of data channels in the underlying dataset.
It differs from general-purpose CPU caches by being implemented as a GPU-resident texture managed via LRU replacement using WebGPU compute passes.
Choose it for modern GPU-driven rendering pipelines requiring texture-based cache access.
This method enables the GPU to steer CPU-side data loading for voxel rendering by reporting node usage, thereby eliminating the overhead of CPU-driven visibility queries and tree traversal.

It builds on [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) by unifying the management of the brick pool and node pool into two LRU-controlled caches where the GPU determines refinement needs and missing data, rather than relying on occlusion queries or frustum containment checks performed on the CPU.
Choose it when minimizing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead is critical.

LRU Cache Management for Voxel Bricks is a memory management strategy that prioritizes reusing voxel brick data that has not been accessed for the longest time, thereby optimizing memory reuse while retaining useful data in the cache.
It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity and transfer bandwidth by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized.

Unlike sibling methods that may rely on hardware-specific features or different replacement policies, this approach explicitly manages the cache lifecycle using a Last Recently Used (LRU) policy, often requiring CPU-side coordination due to the limitations of standard shader models regarding random memory writes.
Choose it for standard shader models lacking hardware cache management.
CPU DRAM serves as a warm cache between SSD storage and GPU VRAM, maintaining an LRU cache over volume blocks with per-block dirty bits.
It decouples GPU residency from SSD write latency by staging evicted blocks in CPU memory before persisting them, turning frequent small updates into batched sequential appends.

This method builds on [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) by adding a write-back policy that distinguishes between clean and dirty blocks, preventing unnecessary SSD writes for blocks that are still being actively reused.
Choose it for out-of-core training or editing pipelines where data persistence matters.
